translation:
These are that person's words — that indeed is what must be said. The sense of this line is that "that person" means one who knows Parbrahma, or who is near to Parbrahma, and the words spoken directly from his own mouth — here a more detailed and clear discussion is being carried on about Parbrahma. Let us begin with the form that Mahadevji himself described, in the raga Malini.

_asitagirisamam syat kajjalam sindhupatre_
_suratatuvarashakhalekhini patramurvim_
_likhati yadi grihitva sharada sarvakalam_
_tadapi tava gunanamisha param na yati_ ||21||
(Mahimnastotra – 32)

(If the ocean were the inkpot, holding collyrium as black as a mountain, if a branch of the wish-granting tree were the pen and the whole earth the paper, and if, taking up all this, the goddess Sharada were to keep writing through every age — even then, O Lord, she could never reach the far shore of Your virtues.)

If the ocean's basin were the inkpot, holding collyrium as black as mountains, and the branches of the wish-fulfilling trees were the pens, and the whole earth were paper, and with all these means Sharada were to go on writing through every age — even then, O God, she would not reach the limit of Your virtues.

Baba Kabirji has a sakhi (couplet):

_kabir kagad thoda gun ghana. kis bidh likhu banay ||_
_sayarmein pani ghana. vo gagri kaise samay ||1||_

(Meaning: Baba Kabirji says the paper is little and God's virtues are many, so how can he write them down briefly? Just as the sea holds so much water that it cannot fit into a small pot, so too God's virtues cannot be written down on so little paper.)

Meaning: Baba Kabirji says paper is scarce and God's virtues are many, so how is he to write them down in brief? Just as the ocean holds so much water that it could never fit into a small pitcher, so the virtues of God cannot be written down on so little paper.

The purport is that a full description of Parbrahma is not merely extremely difficult but impossible — for who could be capable of knowing His complete works and form? On this matter there is a related sakhi of Baba Kabirji.

_kabir dharatika kagad karu. lekhan karu banaray ||_
_saat samudraki mas karu. to hari gun likha na jaay ||1||_
(Samarath Ras – 61-5)

(Kabirji says: even if I were to make the earth into paper, turn all the vegetation upon it into a pen, and make ink out of the waters of the seven seas, still I could not write a full description of Parbrahma.)

Kabirji says that were he to make the earth into paper, and make a pen from all the vegetation upon the earth, and make ink as much as the water of the seven oceans, even then he could not write a description of Parbrahma. This same point is made in the Bhagavad Gita as well; it also appears in the Bhagavat. Further, Mahadevji too has described this Parbrahma, who is beyond the three gunas. He said to Parvatiji: listen to a description of my Vasudev.

_niranjano niralambo nirlepyo nirvinigrahah ||_
_nirguno nirvikalpo'thaabhayo'nanto'chalo'chyutah ||22||_

(The Lord is Niranjan — stainless; Niralamb — without support; Nirlep — unattached; without any restraint (nigrah); without gunas (vikalp); and He is Abhay — fearless; Anant — infinite; Achal — unmoving; and Achyut — imperishable.)

That is to say: Anjan-bhag (maya) is the name given to a body — the condition (upadhi), that is, the body upon which the smear (lep) of maya's collyrium (anjan) has not fallen, is called Niranjan; here "body" itself is spoken of as maya. One who, though embodied, remains videha — detached from the body — who has not fallen into maya, who is not entangled in it, is Niranjan. Niralamba — (nir + a + lamba) — one who has never taken the support (alamban, prop) of anyone else. One who has never, not even once, anywhere, accepted the support, prop, or refuge of another — that is the meaning here. In the gross sense it is not meant that one soul (jiva) helps another jiva; rather, the sole shelterer of the jiva is Parbrahma. In worldly dealings, support or help carries this gross meaning, but after coming into human birth, a person has not gone off into dependence on anyone else — worshipping other gods and goddesses (anadev), getting entangled in tantra-mantra, threads and charms. It is in this sense that the matter is to be understood here, as it has been explained in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad —

_atha yo'nyam devatamupaste'nyo'savanyo'hamasmiti_
_na sa veda yatha pashurevamsa devanam. yatha ha vai_
_bahavah pashavo manushyam bhunjyuyurevamekaikah purusho devanbhu_
_naktyekasminnaiva pashavadiyamane'priyam bhavati kimu_
_bahushu tasmadeshaan tanna priyam yadetanmanushya vidyuh ||1||_
(Brihadaranyaka – 1-4-10)

(One who worships another deity, thinking "he is other and I am other," does not know the truth. His state is like that of an animal belonging to the gods. Just as many animals together sustain one man, so each person sustains the gods through his worship of them. If even one animal is taken from its owner it displeases him — how much more so if many are taken. So this too [men abandoning their worship] does not please the gods.)

The person who worships another god, holding that "I am one and the gods are another," does not know the true matter. Such people's condition is like animals belonging to the gods. Just as many animals together sustain a man, so each person, by worshipping the gods, sustains the gods. If someone takes away even one animal it does not please its owner — how much less would it please him if many animals were taken? In the same way the gods too do not like this happening (men giving up their worship of them).

The meaning is that the lesser gods (anadev) can live only on the offerings (tarpan) of human beings. They too must enter the cycle of birth and death; when their merit is exhausted they too must take birth again. What is said here about niralamb is meant in this sense — one who has never, in worship or service, taken the shelter of anyone but Parbrahma — that alone is Niralamb.

Sin, merit, joy, sorrow, elation, grief, delusion, envy, greed, ego, lust, and anger do not touch him; all the senses, the five elements, the three gunas, and this whole creation and universe cannot obstruct him, cannot hinder him, cannot raise any difficulty for him — know this to be Nirvigraha, one beyond restraint or opposition. Rajas, Tamas and Sattva are the three gunas; where their maya does not touch, and the doer-person of these three gunas (Parbrahma) is Nirgun, without gunas. Where, even for time itself, this body of limbs (of flesh) does not become sustenance — meaning: hands, feet, mouth, head, eyes, and all of it — where He takes on no part or limb of a body at all — that should be known as Nirvikalpa, one without alternative form.

The purport meant here is that the limbs or senses by which the presence of a body is perceived are perishable, but it is not fitting to imagine such a thing of Parbrahma. "The Lord of all the worlds alone reigns and plays, without a body" — from the kadvu (a devotional verse-canto). He is one who is bodiless; hence He has been called Nirvikalp, for there is none other like Him. Parbrahma alone is all-powerful. Here Adhyaruji Maharaj says —

_rup arupe janiye. ane naam vade de par ||_
_narayan naam ocharo. joi lejo saar ||1||_
(Kirtan 13-15)

(Do not seek to know Him through debating form and formlessness; only by the Name can you cross over. Utter the Name "Narayan," and see — take in its essence.)

There is no need to fall into the dispute of form versus formlessness in order to know the Supreme. Only through the Name should you know Him — and Adhyaruji Maharaj says: utter the name "Narayan," and then see what fruit, what essence, comes of it.

One who has no fear of anyone is Abhay. The Supreme has been called Abhay. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says —

_so'bibhettasmat ekaki bibheti sahayamikshaam_
_chakre yanmadanyannnasti kasmanu vibhemiti tat evasya_
_bhayam viyaaya kasmadvyabheshyad dvitiyadvai bhayam bhavati ||2||_
(1-4-2)

(He became afraid; that is why one who is alone feels afraid. But he reflected: since there is nothing apart from Me, of whom should I be afraid? — and at that his fear departed. But why was he afraid at all? For fear indeed arises only from something other than oneself.)

That Brahma became afraid; therefore a person who is alone feels afraid. But he reflected: apart from Me there is nothing else, so of whom should I be afraid? — and then his fear left him. But why was he afraid in the first place? Fear indeed arises from another. Jivanji Maharaj has not accepted this independent capability of Brahma. He has not upheld the Vedantic teaching of worshipping Brahma; rather, Jivanji Maharaj explains the worship of Parbrahma, who is beyond even Brahma — that is why He alone is called Abhay, one who fears nothing.

That very Being can be Arup, formless, who, without form, performs crores and thousands of works in the universe — His, the formless Parbrahma's, contemplation and worship never go in vain. That is: though He is without colour or form, He remains ever ready to help in His devotees' undertakings — that is why He is also called Bhakta Vatsal, affectionate toward devotees.

_bhakt vatsal biru taharu. tuhaj garuo raay ||_
_lila sabli taahari. te varanan kehi pere thaay ||3||_

(Bhakta Vatsal is Your very title; You alone, O King, are great. Your play is so mighty — how could it ever be described?)

Further, another name of His is Achal, unmoving, for even at the end of the ages (kalpas) He remains unchanged, unshifting, unaltered — He is Achal. These are the very words of the great Rudra. As the testimony of the Vishnu scriptures bears witness, Shri Krishna, free of the three gunas, is truly this very Morli Manohar Parmeshwar — the flute-charming Supreme Lord. Kabirji bears witness to this —

_kabir ekahi akhar alakhse. maatra mile chhatris ||_
_rajas uthe sat likhe. sankele tam ish ||2||_

_kabir mor mugat pankaj nayan. kundal makaraakar ||_
_so murat mere nayana baso. chitmein karo vihaar ||3||_

Meaning: from that one undying syllable (akshar) of the Supreme — which cannot be known through vowels and consonants, nor written in words — thirty-six matras (measures) come forth. Within it, creation comes about in the world through God's rajasik disposition; through the satvik disposition its sustenance takes place; and the tamasik disposition of that Lord gathers the creation back into Himself, draws it back within Himself.

In the three gunas, each of the three gunas has twelve aspects (ang), and so 12 × 3 = 36 — the total aspects of the gunas come to thirty-six. Hence Kabirji says —

_kabir baar ang saakarka, baar ang niraakar ||_
_baaro ang niranjani, aur avastha chaar ||2||_

Meaning: the Supreme God's Sakar, embodied, form has twelve aspects, and the Nirakar, formless, form likewise has twelve aspects. All these twelve-and-twelve aspects belong to the God who is beyond maya, and in His creation there are four states — childhood, youth, adulthood, and old age. In keeping with this sakhi, Kabir says in another sakhi —

_kabir panch tatvako vraksh hai, trigunaka vistaar ||_
_rajas uthai tam khapai, saatvik samdhaar ||3||_

Meaning: the five elements form a tree, which has spread and expanded through the three gunas; that tree rises and grows through the rajas guna, dissolves through the tamas guna, while through the sattva guna it endures evenly from its rise to its end. If the Supreme's one syllable is reckoned as Om, it has eight matra-portions, and all eight together make one matra. Further, there are six ragas, each of which has six raginis (its consorts) —

Bindu — 1/2 matra
Ardhachandra — 1/4 matra
Nirodhini — 1/8 matra
Nad — 1/16 matra
Nadant — 1/32 matra
Shakti — 1/64 matra
Vyapini — 1/128 matra
Samana — 1/128 matra
Jod — 1 matra

— thus, in this way too, the matras of a single syllable can be counted as thirty-six. But for us, Kabirji, addressing the worldly conduct that runs by the rule of the three gunas, speaks of these thirty-six matras for those attached and coloured in the love of maya, given over to lust. But Kabirji's own devotion is toward Shri Krishna. Hence, in a sakhi, Kabirji says: he whose crown is a peacock feather, whose eyes are like lotuses, whose earrings sway like fish — may that form of Shri Krishna dwell within my sight, and may contemplation of it go on continually within my mind — this is what he wishes.

In the three pranayamas — Rechak, Kumbhak and Purak — Purak (inhalation) is filled with 4, 8 and 16 matras; then Kumbhak (retention) is filled with 16, 64 and 32 matras; and Rechak (exhalation) is carried out with 8, 32 and 16 matras. But pointing to such matras and to the three gunas and so forth, Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj, through Kabir's sakhi, counsels only the contemplation and meditation of Shri Krishna alone.

The revered Yadunath Maharaj, in his exposition of this Kabir sakhi of the "one undying syllable," has written: in life, when the rajasik disposition arises, it should be suppressed with the sattvik, and in the same way the tamas guna too should be gathered in and suppressed — the unknowable Alakh cannot be known, and it is from that very Alakh that all the languages of the world have come into being.

Meaning: the three great gods together made this creation by means of the three gunas, and the three of them divided the work among themselves — Brahma for creation, Vishnu for sustenance, Shiva for destruction. But the Parbrahma, crowned with a peacock's feathers, wearing golden earrings, may He dwell within the very pupils of my eyes. Vyasji, the foremost worshipper of Parbrahma Shri Krishna and eternal resident of Vrindavan, says —

_vyas jake kie tin gun. tatva aur chobis ||_
_ta mohanku govalani. phul chugave sis ||4||_

Meaning: He who has made the three gunas and the five elements, and who has also fashioned the five elements and the twenty-four qualities — that same all-capable Morli Manohar Parmeshwar, Shri Krishna, that Mohan — upon his head the cowherdesses lovingly offer flowers. There Kabirji says — there is a sakhi about how Shri Krishna remains under the sway of the innocent Gopis.

_bed bhed jaane nahi, neti neti kahai bain ||_
_ta mohanso raadhika, kahai mahaavaru dain ||4||_

Meaning: to that Shri Krishna, whose mystery even the Vedas do not know, and whom even the Vedas, unable to grasp His secret, can only describe as "not this, not this" (neti neti), Radhikaji says: apply mahavar to my feet — mahavar being the red dye that fortunate, married women apply to their feet.

_jaahi raaha pandit gaye, taahi gai baahar ||_
_uchi ghati naamki, taha chadh raha kabir ||5||_

Meaning: the path of knowledge, action, yoga, the Vedas, and ritual observance — that path the pandits took, but that road lay outside the true attainment of God. The road to the attainment of God is the road of the high mountain pass — the mountain path of "Ram Nam," the Name of Ram. Kabirji, for his part, is climbing that very path.

_jagat nachaayo baandhke, tin gunke dor ||_
_toku gokul govaalani, pakar nachave por ||6||_

Meaning: He who has bound and made the whole world dance with the thread of the three gunas — that same Shri Krishna is seized by the Gopis of Gokul and made to dance and play in the lanes of Gokul.

_kabir je van pavan na sanchare. pankhi koe na jaay ||_
_so van kabire dhundhiya jahaan. krishna charave gaay ||5||_
(Kasoti – 10-26)

In the forest so dense that even the wind cannot pass through its countless trees, where not even a single bird can dwell, Kabirji says that in such an inaccessible forest, Krishna grazes his cows. That is, Kabirji has discovered a forest which is supreme devotion (bhakti) itself, where no other worshippers can enter. Only he can come there who, having renounced everything else, every other form of worship, has attained supreme devotion alone — only he can reach this state.

This is the abode of the Lord's play, His forest. The wind stands for the individual souls (jivatmas). The bird stands for the mind. The cows He grazes stand for the senses — this sakhi is presented as such an allegory.

_kabir agam agochar gam nahi. jahaan jhalmal jyot ||_
_taha das kabira bandagi. jahaan paap pun nahi chhot ||6||_

Kabirji says: to know the form of Parbrahma, even the agam (the inaccessible — the Vedic scriptures and the like) and the agochar (the imperceptible — the senses and the like) find no understanding. Where the flame-like form of Parbrahma continually flickers and shimmers, none can grasp the way to that agam-agochar light. There, having himself reached such an exalted seat, he performs devotion to that form of Parbrahma, radiant with light, where neither sin nor merit can even enter. This sakhi appears in the Parchari (hagiographic account) of Rankaji in this manner —

_agam agochar gam nahi, taanhaa param sukh bhog ||_
_tiha bhakt jan ram rahya, jaanhaa paap pun nahi chhot ||7||_

Further, in the Sarvang Lila the closing line runs as follows —

_ras ramaadi gopika, hari ade abhade naahi ||_

In this line it is said: though the Lord performed the ras-lila with the Gopis, He remained free of any impurity — He is beyond sin and merit.

There Jivandasji spoke —

_nirgun brahmthe jivana. trigun bhayo vistaar ||_
_sakal gun seva kare. so aap raha niradhaar ||7||_

_trigun rahit gunmaan base. so sadguru diyo bataay ||_
_nirgun brahm vede kahyo. so vraj kul chaare gaay ||8||_

_to nirgun sagun jivana. so vraj kul chaare gaay ||_
_sagun vrikhabhanki daavadi. nirgun jadupati raay ||9||_

Meaning: Nirgun Brahma, that is, Shri Krishna, from whom the three gunas — rajas, tamas, sattva — arose, and all the gunas serve Him: this refers to Brahma, Vishnu, Mahesh, and the like, as well as the Vaishnavas who worship through the three gunas. "He Himself remains niradhar (without any support)" means that Shri Krishna, though He is the one who manifests the three gunas, remains untouched by them.

Jivanji Maharaj says that from Ishwar in His maya-conditioned aspect arose the three gunas — rajas, tamas, sattva — and these gunas serve that maya-conditioned Ishwar; that is his support. But He, Brahma, Parbrahma, is Himself niradhar, without support.

Parmeshwar, who is free of the three gunas, dwells also within the very substance of the three gunas. The existence of the three gunas has no separate existence apart from Parmeshwar — this the Sadguru has explained. The three gunas are subject to Parmeshwar. The Vedas call this Parbrahma Nirgun, beyond all gunas — yet that very God grazes cows in the abode of Vraj-kul, Vrindavan; He conducts the running of creation. There is no separate doer in Him — in that sense the Vaishnava who is gunatit, beyond the gunas, is a servant of Govind, gunatit like Krishna himself. That Supreme, who is both Nirgun and Sagun, that very Krishna grazes cows in Vraj-mandal. In this, God's Sagun form is Radhika, daughter of Vrishabhanu, and His Nirgun form is Shri Krishna, foremost of the Yadu clan.

That is: Brahma is Nirgun, unattached; Brahma does nothing at all, and yet the whole universe is wrapped around Him. Brahma Himself, though free of gunas, is that by whose influence alone everything else becomes active. The Sadguru has given us sight of such a Brahma. A lengthy discussion of the subject of Brahma will not be carried on here, but this very Nirgun Brahma grazes cows in Vraj-kul. Brahma's Sagun form is Radhaji, and His Nirgun form is Krishna.

_mayadhyakshena prakritih suyate sacharacharam ||_
_hetunanena kaunteya jagadviparivartate ||3||_
(Gita 9-10)

("O Kaunteya [Arjuna]! Under My — Krishna-Parbrahma's — superintendence Prakriti brings forth all that moves and does not move, and by this cause the universe undergoes its changes.")

"O Kaunteya (Arjuna)! Under My (Krishna-Parbrahma's) governance Prakriti conducts its manifold workings, and by that very means the world undergoes transformation."

_ek vishese jaaniye. ne dip vant akaar ||_
_ras paatra vrit paharaari. anjan saheja nivaar ||29||_
(Harsh Bhavan 29)

Prakriti has three gunas; though the three gunas are mutually opposed in nature to one another, worldly activity, creation, proceeds only through the union of all three. Just as oil, wick (cotton) and fire, though of opposite natures, give light only through the combination of all three — for oil alone does not burn, nor does cotton alone — yet where an unbroken lamp is burning, the cotton within the flame is not consumed even as the oil slowly burns away and gives light. In this way, though the three gunas are of opposing natures, the workings of the world could not proceed without even one of them.

_eko devah sarvabhuteshu gudhah sarvavyaapi sarvabhutantaraatma ||_
_karmaadhyaksah sarvabhutaadivaasah saakshi cheta kevalo nirgunashcha ||4||_
(Shvetashvatara Upanishad – 6-11)

(This one God dwells hidden in all beings; He is all-pervading, the inner self of all beings, the overseer of all works, the abode of all beings, the witness, the pure consciousness, and He alone is without gunas.)

This one, hidden Parbrahma dwells in all beings (humans and others), and this Brahma, dwelling within all beings, is the foremost witness of their actions, and He alone is entirely Nirgun.

That is: though dwelling together with Prakriti, who possesses the gunas, He is Nirgun — the gunas do not touch Him. Parbrahma is only the witness of it all; He is merely the doer, the maker of the whole world and so forth — nothing at all touches Him. Further, as was said earlier, that the Nirgun Brahma is spoken of in the Vedas — in the tenth mandala of the Rigveda, in speaking of the origin of creation, it is said —

_ko addhaavedakaihapravochatkuta aajaataakuta iyam visrishtih ||_
_arvaagdeva asyavisarjanenaathaakovedayata aabubhuva ||5||_
(Rigveda 10-129-6)

Who truly knows the elements of Prakriti? Who can describe them? By whose union — whose worship — did this creation come into being? For what cause did this manifold creation arise? The gods and the like too are themselves born as an inner part of this very creation — who then knows from where creation itself arose?

_iyam visrishtiryataabubhuvayadivaadadheyadivaanam ||_
_yo asyaadhyakshah paramevyoman tso adgavedayadivaanaveda ||6||_
(10-129-7)

"From where did this manifold creation arise? Who created it, and who did not create it? All this only he can know who dwells in the very own abode of Parbrahma-Parmeshwar. It may well be that even they — the gods and the like, Narad and others — do not know this."

In the Mahabharata there is a dialogue between Sanatkumar and Narad, in which Narad falls into delusion. But here one thing is worth noting: in the matter of the creation of the universe, the highest place has not been given to the gods Agni and Indra. The Brahma spoken of in Vedanta, Jivanji Maharaj has treated as secondary, and has shown Parbrahma's true form to be that which is even beyond Brahma. It is this form, beyond even Brahma, of which Jivanji Maharaj speaks — and Adhyaruji Maharaj too has expressed this very idea, most simply, in a verse of his kadvu. He has stated it so effortlessly that one would hardly realise what great, hidden mystery lies behind it.

_chidaanandam parabrahma dhyaanagamyam sanaatanam ||_
_aksharam nirmalam nityam niraakaram namaamyaham ||7||_

(I bow to that Parbrahma-Parmatma, who is of the nature of consciousness and bliss, attainable through meditation, eternal, imperishable (akshar), stainless, everlasting, and formless.)

I bow to the Parbrahma-Parmatma who is of the nature of knowledge and bliss, who can be experienced through meditation, who is sanatan (everlasting), akshar (imperishable), free of impurity, eternal, and formless.

_sur muni antariksh stave re gokul. hari te ati re akal ||_
_hari hari rame re govind aanand bharyo e ||1||_
_aapanape ramato pindaara ramaade. hari te rame ne ramaade ||_
_harite jame ne jamaade. harino gagan brahmaadik vichaar kare e ||2||_
_akal ramat maandi gokul maahen. ramat brahmaadik chaahe_
_hari te aapanape ade na abhade e. ||3||_

That is: Adhyaruji Maharaj clearly declares that this is the inconceivable play (lila) of Parbrahma, difficult to understand, bewildering even for Brahma and the other gods. The Vedantis (Shankaracharya and others), unable to grasp it, call this the "maya" of Brahma, while Vallabhacharya recognises it as the "lila" of Brahma. Further, Ramanujacharya sees this kind of form of Brahma as vishishtha — that is, as a wondrous form. But Jivanji Maharaj, Adhyaruji, and others mean by it that for Him anything at all in the world is possible; He holds every kind of power. Moreover, He remains pervading everywhere throughout the universe. What is spoken of as His cosmic (virat) form in the Puranas and in the Gita is this very form. And yet, more than the other acharyas, the saints of the Ramkabir tradition — from Gyaniji down to Jivanji, Padmanabh, and others — have not entered into the dispute over Parbrahma's form versus formlessness, but rather, having reconciled the two, have seen Parbrahma in both forms together. And yet no gross idol has been given a place or recognition in this tradition. Here a sakhi of Rankaji is given —

_ghareku dhijoon nahi. esa paaya naaka ||_
_aakaar niraakaar vivarjit. taaka sevak ranka ||10||_

_ghareku dhijoon sahi. rahoo adharke maahen ||_
_wanka taha vilambia. jaha dhoop nahi chhaay ||11||_

Meaning: this is a dialogue between the husband Ranka and the wife Vanka concerning God, given across these two sakhis. In it Ranka says: even were you to say that God takes on a Sakar, embodied, idol-form, still, however many attempts you make to persuade me that God dwells in this Sakar, embodying form, I will not accept what you say — I will not be swayed at all, because I have now obtained the most minute, subtle knowledge of exactly where the Supreme is to be found — that is, I have now come to full knowledge about God — so that I have now become this Ranka, the worshipper and devotee of that divine essence which is free of both Sagun-Sakar (embodied, qualified) and Nirgun-Nirakar (unembodied, unqualified).

Meaning: in answer, seemingly in contradiction and yet, in fact, supporting her husband's view by an inverse route, Ranka's devoted wife Vanka speaks. She says: O Ranka, though you may deny it, I for my part will indeed accept God's Sagun-Sakar form. But my loving devotion I will surely keep fixed upon the Nirgun-Nirakar — that is, though God can manifest as either the Sagun or the Nirgun principle, He Himself remains detached from both Sagun and Nirgun, and it is upon that divine essence that I shall fix my mind, says Vanka. I shall remain in the shelter and refuge of that very divine essence, where there is no such thing at all as sunshine or shade — that is, no such pair of opposites as joy and sorrow.

Ranka Bhagat says: material things are perishable; he places no trust in such things — this is the teaching, the guiding mark, that his Guru has shown him. He, Ranka Bhagat, is the servant of that Supreme who is the support of all, who has no fixed form, and for whom not even the notion of formlessness applies.

Vanka Bhagat says: today's perishable, material things — nothing can be accomplished without them, for performing devotion, receiving teaching, practising religious discipline, and carrying out activity cannot happen without the body. Therefore, for these purposes, she does hold the body as necessary — but her disposition (vritti) she keeps fixed on that support-less Supreme who is the support of all. In Him her disposition has become steady. What is that Supreme like? Where there is no shade, no sunshine, no joy or sorrow, but only the very nature of supreme bliss.

Rankaji, being extremely poor, his real name has been forgotten, and he came to be known by the name "Ranka" (meaning pauper). His wife too, though devoted to her husband, was, so to speak, positive-negative — the reverse-and-obverse of him — for Vanka would speak the opposite (vanku, crooked) of what Ranka said, yet her intention was always to lend support to Ranka himself, and for this crooked manner of speaking she became known by the name "Vanka." But the presentations of Ranka and Vanka are like two sides of a single coin, each true in its own way. When Rankaji refused to accept the Sakar, Vanka did not deny the Sakar but accepted it — yet did so in a roundabout way that ultimately lent support to Ranka's own position.

Sadguru Jivanji Maharaj's guru Gopaldas had four principal disciples, among whom was Anantdas of Borbar. He composed the Parcharis (hagiographic accounts) of nine saints in all. He held a line of thought that endorsed Jivanji Maharaj's own principles, and so he drew important sayings from the Parcharis of Namdevji and Pipaji into the Samagam. Here, then, let us look at a few verses from the Ranka-Vanka Parchari composed by Anantdas, in which there is material corresponding to these sakhis.

In this Parchari there is a small dialogue between Namdev and Ranka. Once, when Ranka's daughter had gone to the river to fetch water for worship and service, some drops fell on her water-vessel from Namdev's daughter nearby, upon which Ranka's daughter, quarrelling, said: "Your father practises a stubborn, insistent kind of devotion to God, but God helps His devotee without any need for such insistence — God is never unaware of His devotee's suffering. Therefore a true devotee does not speak out his suffering before God with his own mouth." Hearing this, Namdev came to Ranka and began to ask what fault there was in his own devotion. Then Ranka said: "You made God drink milk, you had God's temple moved, you brought a dead cow back to life — yet you have not attained the true understanding of devotion to God." And, pointing out his shortcoming, he said —

_pey piyo deval phiro, bhakti na aai tohe ||_
_sant puj re namdev, malia chaahe mohe ||8||_

Meaning: you made God drink milk, had His temple moved, yet true devotion to God has still not been attained by you. O Namdev, if you truly wish to attain God, then serve the saints instead. Let us now look at the discussion that follows.

_ta pichhe nirgun sagun katha chalaai, tehi ausar hari asht dve rup dhari aai ||_
_tab ranka kahe suno santajan bhaai, yame kahaakum bhajo so deho bataai ||9||_

Meaning: after that, discussion of Nirgun and Sagun began, in the course of which it was said that God, through His eightfold nature (ashtadha prakriti), the five elements and the three gunas, assumes both the Sagun and the Nirgun form. Then Rankaji asks: brother, listen — of these two, which form will you worship? (The Sagun of the ten avatars — the one who drank milk, who had the temple moved, who revived the dead cow — or the Nirgun?)

_dash kaho to hari dash naahi, ek kaho to nav kahaan samaai ||_
_tab namdevake man bhayo bicharu, yame kahaakum kahu kiratharu ||10||_

Meaning: if you say God has ten avatars, then He is not merely ten; and if you say God is only One, then where would the other nine be accommodated? At this, Namdev's mind fell to pondering which of these two alternatives he should call God.

_dekh charitra chit bhaari, kachu samajh na pare he harirai ||_
_tab ranke aad avinaashi diya jataai, naamarupki bhakti kahi samjhaai ||11||_

Meaning: seeing this bewildering conduct of God, Namdev's mind fell into great confusion, and he could make no sense at all of the matter of Hariraya. Then Ranka made known and explained to him the primordial, imperishable, complete Parbrahma-Parmatma, and explained to him how devotion to the Name-and-Form should be performed.

_rup naam shiv sanakaadik phunipati jaane, dhru prahlaad dhyaan man aane ||_
_vaanchhit bhakt kare chit laai, dini bhakt mukt vaikunth pad paai ||12||_

Meaning: Shiv, the Sanakadik sages, and Sheshnag with his thousand hoods all know how to perform devotion to the Name-and-Form. Dhruv and Prahlad too fix their minds in contemplation of Him. In this way devotees perform devotion with an eye toward the fruit they desire, and to such devotees God grants liberation and the state of Vaikunth.

_naam rupki bhakt kahi samjhaai, tab hari kala lai samaai ||_
_ek anek rup dhari aave, mool graha bina bharam na jaave ||13||_

Meaning: when devotion to the Name-and-Form had been explained, it was understood where God's kala (portion, aspect) finds its accommodation — that the one Supreme comes assuming many forms. Hence, without understanding God's true, original form, illusion cannot depart.

_daria lahera dve kachu naahin, upaje anek phuni tahanhi samaai ||_
_itani goshta bhai naamako man maanyo, ranakaku sadguru kahi pramaano ||14||_

Meaning: the ocean and its waves are not two separate things — many waves arise in the ocean and merge back into it again. In the same way there is no separateness between God and His avatars. Once this much discussion had taken place, Namdev's mind was satisfied, and he acknowledged Ranka as his Sadguru.

Meaning: he will not trust, will not be swayed by, will not give weight to the form the Supreme takes on — he cares nothing for form, he will not accept the Sagun principle as the ultimate God.

In the tradition, Rankaji and Vankaji are famed together as a couple of devotees. Their special quality is that they present every matter in an inverted manner — that is, speaking in terms of language, their statements are always couched in a figure of paronomasia (shlesh). Here too they explain, in the same beautiful language, that "Gharekoo" refers to the matter of Parbrahma — that is, for the sake of Parbrahma's Sagun-Sakar worship he cannot keep his patience; he does not waste time, nor allow any kind of delay — such is his resolve, that without falling into debates over form and formlessness he has never stopped or slowed the pace of his worship. Whereas Rankaji's wife says that she does not perform the worship of Parbrahma hastily, without knowing and understanding it — she chooses her path of worship and devotion with all seriousness; she remains within her worship of both the Sagun and the Nirgun, and of that which is beyond both — her Parmeshwar is beyond both sunshine (form) and shade (formlessness).

Thus, though expressed each in their own style, both are conveying the same single point — that in choosing one's path of worship one ought not to waste time. This is the inner intent conveyed here. And yet, to wander about anywhere at all, without knowing or understanding anything, is likewise sheer folly, tantamount to self-destruction — for time waits for no one, and the path of devotion must always remain free of dispute. Devotion alone should be the mantra of life; not the slightest scholarly pedantry has any place in devotion, and further, for the path of devotion one must become free of ego — ego is the greatest gateway to downfall on the path of devotion. Therefore one should worship the innocent, faultless Parbrahma rather than scriptures or abstruse learning, without leaning on any prop whatsoever, and devotees should never allow any delay in their devotion either.

(Rankaji was born in Pandharpur in Vikram Samvat 1347, Magshar Sud 2. Vankaji was born in Pandharpur in Vikram Samvat 1351, Vaishakh Vad 7.)

_niraakaar niradhaar hai. aakaare aanand ||_
_god khelaave jashomati. so puran parmaanand ||12||_

_e rup arupe shaamalo. khele nand dwaar ||_
_aadi omkaar upanyo jivana. koti brahmaand vistaar ||13||_

_niraakaar aakaarthe. adbhut ek arup ||_
_so saai hamaare jivana. je sitaapatiko rup ||14||_

Meaning: the Nirakar, formless, needs no support of form; hence in the worship of a Nirgun God, one cannot enjoy the flavour of love. But when devotion is performed to the Sagun form, one may take pleasure in the joy of love in relation to Him. Such is the Lord Krishna of Sagun-Sakar form, whom Jashodaji plays with in her lap as her son — the same Krishna who is Himself of the nature of supreme bliss. — 11

This dark-complexioned (shyamal) Krishna, who is of embodied form and yet, as formless, is also without any form, plays as a child in Nandji's palace. Jivanji Maharaj says that this very Krishna precedes even the Omkari, triguni creation itself — it was from this Parmatma Krishna that the crores of triguni universes first spread into expansion. — 12

Jivanji Maharaj says: the God who is astonishing beyond even Nirgun-Nirakar and Sagun-Sakar, who is without any form at all — such is our object of worship, who abides in the form of Sitapati Ram. — 13

In discussing the form of Parbrahma, Jivanji Maharaj, further ahead in this same section, explains the matter of Nirgun Brahma; now here he explains the matter of this Nirgun Brahma's Sakar form — the Nirakar Parbrahma has been called Niradhar, without support or foundation, for even Parbrahma, in order to act — that is, for the protection of His devotees — must come, out of the formless, into a form, into some definite mould or shape. Hence the Nirakar form too merges back into the complete Brahma; Brahma's Sakar form is but a portion of Parbrahma. For instance, Krishna's form was of the thirtieth part — a partial manifestation. Thus one must understand the complete form of Parbrahma, which not every soul (jiva) has the capacity to behold. Furthermore, since Parbrahma is present within all elements and within every kind of nature (prakriti), by what form is He to be recognised? Here, in the pad of Brahmaruli, Adhyaruji Maharaj says —

_vaayu gandh maahen sanchare. ture brahmaaruli || gandh muke nij rup ||35||_
_tem hari gunmaan sanchare || ture brahmaaruli || nirgun jape tuj naam ||36||_

Meaning: in every single thing — trees, leaves, fruit, flowers, the earth, and so on — there is a scent, and the wind enters into that scent and spreads it. In the same way, the scent that resides in a tree, its fruit, its flowers, leaves its own original source-form of tree, leaf and fruit, and diffuses into the wind — so too you make your own existence merge into Parbrahma, the ruler of the universe. In the very same way God too enters into the three gunas, and this Nirgun-Nirakar Parbrahma keeps repeating your Name and Form. So too you make your own existence merge into Parbrahma, the ruler of the universe.

That is: Parbrahma spreads through the air like scent, and in the same way Parbrahma pervades and abides everywhere. That is why it is extremely difficult to identify Parbrahma with any fixed form, whether Akar or Nirakar.

_gnaan vairaagya toran karya. ane sthabham shankar brahm ||_
_nishkarma bhakti hidoladdo. hidolare hiche hiche hari parabrahm ||_

He made a torana (a festive canopy, here a cradle-frame) of knowledge and detachment, and made Shankar and Brahma its two pillars; and in this cradle, Parbrahma lies asleep. That is to say: the cradle of nishkarsh (neutral gear) does not turn in the round of birth and death — this state is called Nishkarma Bhakti, action-free devotion.

Adhyaruji Maharaj says in the Vadi Ras —

_rahyo vyaapi vishvasthaapi. gopavyu te naam ||_
_shambh bambh bolaavia. behunne sopya kaam ||1||_

Meaning: after the work of creating the universe, He called upon Shiva and the other gods and entrusted the tasks to them, while He Himself, though pervading and abiding everywhere, remained hidden — that is, apart. His name too is secret. When He gave Adhyaruji Maharaj a vision, he came to know that Parbrahma by the name "Padmanabh."

If we take the discussion of Akar-Nirakar further here, then, as Jivanji Maharaj has already said in an earlier sakhi, "Aadi Onkar Upajyo" (in the beginning arose the Omkar) — meaning that the maker of the world is one Parmeshwar alone, but in this world the jivatmas (individual souls) have divided themselves into two groups: (1) those jivatmas who, having come into this world, have managed to preserve their identity (tadatmya) with Parbrahma even while engaged in worldly action — these Jivanji Maharaj has identified by the term "Sadguru's family" (Sadguruko Parivar); and (2) those jivatmas who have become entangled with the Prakriti-maya pervading this world and have forgotten Parbrahma, the maker of the world — for such jivatmas Jivanji Maharaj has used the term "Onkari creation." This matter has been explained at length in the Parchari of Krishnadasji. Kabirji, describing this, says that in the world different sects and traditions each present their own preferred form of worship — such as worship of the form of Light, Onkar, Yoga, meditation, worship of goddesses, ritual observance (karmakand), the three gunas as deities, places of pilgrimage, vows, family deities, the Vedas, the Puranas, homa, havan, yajna, Mahamaya, the moon, the sun, the siddhis, astrology, and so on and so forth — people fall into, scatter among, or wander through such things. But no one has ever truly known the movement (gati) of Hari. Kabirji, however, points to the Rarankar —

_kabir rarankaar bataave. aur baatke nikat na jaave ||_
_niramal bhakti ja janako hoi. hari rahet ta ghatmein goi ||_
_niramal bhakti kabir j kini. ta ghat vaas kiyo hari cheni ||_
_rarankaar rup dhari jaave. taha kabir sangh chali aave ||_

(Kabir points only to the Rarankar; he draws near to no other matter. Whoever attains flawless devotion — Hari abides hidden within that person's heart. Kabir himself has performed this flawless devotion; the awakened Hari has made His abode within that heart. Wherever Hari appears, taking on the form of Rarankar, there Kabir's own fellowship comes walking along and arrives.)
